rules.rule_en: The Positive Degree is used to express or describe a characteristic of a noun.
The Comparative Degree is used when two things are compared.
The Superlative Degree is used when more than two things are compared and singles out one from the rest.
Adjectives often form comparative by adding -er and superlative by adding -est.
Adjectives ending in 'y' change to 'ier' and 'iest'.
One-syllable adjectives ending in a consonant often double the final consonant before adding -er/-est.
Longer adjectives use 'more' for comparative and 'most' for superlative.
When the positive degree ends in e, only r is added to make it comparative and only st is added to make it superlative.
Ends in y changed into i before adding er and est.
Ends in a single consonant, preceded by a short vowel, this consonant doubles before adding er and est.
Adjectives of more than two syllables, and many of those with two, form the comparative by using 'more' with the positive, and the superlative by using 'most' with the positive.

Elder and eldest are used only of persons, not of animal or things; and are confined to members of the same family. Elder is not used with 'than'. Older and oldest are used for both persons and things.
Adjectives ending in -or are followed by the preposition 'to'.
A great many adjectives and a few adverbs form their comparatives and superlatives by adding -er and -est respectively.
Some adjectives and adverbs take 'more' and 'most' to form their comparatives and superlatives.
Some adjectives and adverbs take either the former or the latter (e.g. more gentle - most gentle).
A few adjectives and adverbs form their comparatives and superlatives in an irregular way (e.g. good - better - best).
Comparatives ending in -or are followed by 'to' instead of 'than'.
Adjectives in superlative degree are preceded by the definite article 'the'.
The definite article 'the' is often omitted before superlative adverbs.
The definite article 'the' is not used before superlatives that follow a noun in possessive case.
Comparison of equals is expressed by 'as + adjective + as'.
In negative comparison, 'so + adjective + as' is often used instead of 'as + adjective + as'.
Sentences with adjectives and adverbs can be interchanged into different degrees of comparison without changing their meaning.
Type 1: Positive (No other... as noble as) -> Comparative (nobler than any other) -> Superlative (the noblest of all).
Type 2: Positive (Very few... as noble as) -> Comparative (nobler than many other) -> Superlative (one of the noblest).
Standard suffixes -er/-est are added to monosyllabic words like tall (taller/tallest), smart (smarter/smartest), large (larger/largest), big (bigger/biggest), late (later/latest).
There are three ways to compare: positive, comparative, and superlative, known as degrees of comparison.
Adjectives change their form to show how one entity compares to another in terms of a specific quality.
For most one syllable adjectives, add -er to make the comparative form and -est for the superlative form.
If the adjective already ends in e, add only -r for comparative and -st for superlative.
For adjectives with a consonant-vowel-consonant pattern at the end, double the last letter before adding -er or -est.
One syllable adjectives ending in a consonant after a vowel need a double letter before adding -er or -est.
For adjectives ending in y, change the y to an i, then add -er for comparative and -est for superlative.
For words with two syllables or more, add 'more' for comparative and 'most' for superlative.
Positive degree describes one item, Comparative degree compares two items, Superlative degree compares three or more items.
The Positive Degree is used to express or describe a quality or state the characteristic of the noun.
The Comparative Degree is used when two things (or two sets of things) are compared.
The Superlative Degree is used when more than two things are compared.
Use the positive degree when not making a comparison.
Use the comparative degree when comparing two objects or two people.
Use the superlative degree when comparing more than two objects or two people.
Many adjectives and a few adverbs form comparatives and superlatives by adding ‘-er’ and ‘-est’.
A few adjectives and many adverbs take ‘more’ and ‘most’ to form comparatives and superlatives.
Comparative degree adjectives ending in '-or' are followed by 'to' instead of 'than' (e.g., superior to, junior to).
Superlative degree adjectives are generally preceded by the definite article 'the'.
The article 'the' is omitted before superlative adverbs and when the superlative follows a noun in the possessive case.
Comparison of equals uses 'as + adjective + as'; negative comparisons often use 'so + adjective + as'.
Comparative degree adjectives are followed by 'than' for comparison, or 'of' when denoting selection between two.
Use 'the' with comparative degrees to show interdependence between two things.
Positive degree: as adjective as
Comparative degree: adjective than
Superlative degree: the adjective
If the positive ends in two consonants, or in a single consonant preceded by two vowels, er and est are added.
Adverbs of more than one syllable take more and most.
When the Positive ends in e, only r and st are added.
When the Positive ends in y, preceded by a consonant, the y is changed into i before adding er and est.
If the y is preceded by a vowel, the y is not changed to i.
When the Positive is a word of one syllable and ends in a single consonant, preceded by a short vowel, this consonant is doubled before adding er and est.
In all Adjectives of more than two syllables, and in most Adjectives of two syllables, the Comparative is formed by adding ‘more’ and the Superlative is formed by adding ‘most’.
Adjectives ending in ed, ing, re, ful, ous and those with the stress on the first syllable usually take more and the most.
Irregular Adjectives: Comparative and Superlative forms are not formed from the Positive degree.

Type I: Comparison between two people or objects. Only positive and comparative degrees are used. 1. Interchange positions. 2. Swap positive and comparative forms. 3. Change affirmative verbs to negative and vice versa.
Comparison is in a group and we select one person as having the quality in the highest degree.
Comparison is in a group but there are a few who are the best and we select one of them.
Superlative: Australia is the largest island in the world. Comparative: Australia is larger than any other island in the world. Positive: No other island in the world is as large as Australia.
Superlative: New York is one of the most crowded cities in America. Comparative: New York is more crowded than most cities in America. Positive: Very few cities in America are as crowded as New York.
